title: When to denormalize; naming conventions, keys and audit columns
summary: A stored copy of derivable data is a cache: decide what keeps it right before you add it. A value copied at the time of an event is not a copy at all. Conventions for names, keys and audit columns make every table predictable.

examples.title: A stored 'last result': one write path, how it drifts, and a reconciliation query

annotations.note: The copy answers "what happened last" without reading test_runs, which matters on a list of thousands of test cases. It is also a second place where that fact lives; the rest of the example is what that costs.

One statement inserts the run and updates the copy, so both commit or neither does. The last condition lets the copy only move forward: an older run arriving late (a retry, an import) can't overwrite a newer result. If two writers race, the second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock and, under READ COMMITTED, re-checks this WHERE against the updated row.
Any writer that skips the write path causes drift: bulk imports, psql sessions, a second service. Nothing fails. The copy is simply wrong from now on.
The view defines the copy once, in terms of its source. id DESC breaks ties between two runs on the same day, so "latest" is deterministic.

A reconciliation query: recompute, compare, list the differences. IS DISTINCT FROM is NULL-safe; with <> TC-2's NULL against 'passed' would be unknown and the row would be missed. Zero rows is the invariant: run it on a schedule or in integration tests.

The repair reuses the view, so there's one definition of the truth. A trigger on test_runs or a materialized view would need no write path discipline at all, at their own costs (triggers and views lessons).

examples.title: A snapshot is a different fact: the price and KDV rate on the order

annotations.note: The foreign key stays. The copied columns freeze the terms; the reference keeps the identity (which product this was). It also means a product with orders can't be deleted, only retired with a flag.

These look like copies of products.price and products.vat_pct, but they record the terms of this order. An invoice that changes when the price list changes is a bug, and in accounting a legal problem.
A value derived from the same row is the cheap kind of denormalization: a generated column is recomputed by the database on every write and can't be written by hand, so it can't drift.
The INSERT takes the copy itself. The client sends a SKU and a quantity, never a price, so a stale screen or a tampered request can't set what the customer pays.
products says what is true today. Turkey's general KDV rate rose from 18% to 20% in July 2023, and every order from before kept 18.
net_if_joined is what a "fully normalized" design reports for order 1: 298.00 instead of the 258.00 that was charged. Here the join is the bug, and the copy is the correct model.

examples.title: Naming conventions, generated constraint names, audit columns and identifier folding

annotations.note: No single convention matters; consistency does. With id everywhere and <singular>_id for references, every join condition is predictable: test_cases.project_id = projects.id. Plural table names also sidestep reserved words: CREATE TABLE user and CREATE TABLE order are syntax errors, users and orders are fine.
Audit columns are timestamptz (the time zones lesson explains why). now() is the start time of the transaction, so every row written in one transaction shares one created_at.
current_user is the database role. Behind a connection pool it is the application's role for every request, here playground. Store the end user explicitly, as a column the application fills.

Generated names follow <table>_<columns>_<suffix>: pkey, key for UNIQUE, fkey, check. Errors carry the constraint name, so the API's error mapping can key on it; write CONSTRAINT name ... wherever you want to choose it. PG 18 also lists NOT NULL constraints here (contype 'n'), which the filter hides.
updated_at = created_at even after the UPDATE, because a DEFAULT applies to INSERT only. Either every UPDATE sets updated_at = now() itself, or a BEFORE UPDATE trigger does (triggers lesson).

Quoted "TestRuns" keeps its capitals, so every query must quote it forever. Unquoted Ürünler shows the folding rule as this UTF-8 database applies it: Fiyat became fiyat, but the non-ASCII Ü stayed upper case.
ürünler with a lower-case ü is a different name: SQLSTATE 42P01. Lower-case ASCII snake_case avoids both traps; Turkish belongs in the data and in comments, not in identifiers.

use_cases: Lists that show an aggregate on every row (last result, open defect count, member count), read far more often than written
Snapshots of the terms at the time of an event: prices and tax rates on order lines, a test case's title in a signed-off test report
Carrying a parent key down (project_id on test_runs) to filter or index without a join, tied to its source by a composite foreign key
Audit columns (created_at, created_by, updated_at) on every table, so 'when did this row change' doesn't need a log search
strengths: A stored aggregate turns a per-row subquery into a column read, which an ORM-driven list page would otherwise repeat for every row
A snapshot keeps documents reproducible: an invoice printed again in five years says what it said, with no history tables
Kept by the same statement (a data-modifying CTE) or by the database (generated column, composite FK with ON UPDATE CASCADE), a copy is as atomic as the write it depends on
Predictable names and audit columns let tooling, error mapping and a reviewer find their way around any table
weaknesses: Every copy needs a write path to keep it right, and imports, psql sessions or a second service that skip it cause silent drift
Reads get cheaper and writes get dearer: each recorded run now also updates, and row-locks, its test case
Drift isn't an error. You only find it with a reconciliation query that somebody has to remember to run
PostgreSQL accepts any name, quoted or not; conventions hold only as far as review and linting enforce them

pitfalls.title: Denormalizing before measuring
pitfalls.detail: A join on indexed keys is cheap. Copy a value when EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data shows the join or the aggregate is the problem, not in advance.

pitfalls.title: updated_at with only a DEFAULT
pitfalls.detail: The default fills it on INSERT and never again, so every row looks untouched. Set it in every UPDATE, or let a trigger do it.
pitfalls.bad: updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()  -- and nothing else
pitfalls.good: UPDATE test_cases SET title = $1, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $2;  -- or a BEFORE UPDATE trigger

pitfalls.title: current_user as the audit user
pitfalls.detail: Behind a connection pool, every row records the application's database role. Record the person explicitly.
pitfalls.bad: created_by text NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user
pitfalls.good: created_by bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users  -- filled by the application

pitfalls.title: Quoted and non-ASCII identifiers
pitfalls.detail: ORMs and GUI designers that quote mixed-case names make every hand-written query quote them too, and unquoted Turkish letters don't fold the way the ASCII ones do.
pitfalls.good: CREATE TABLE test_runs (...);  CREATE TABLE products (...);

pitfalls.title: Identifiers longer than 63 bytes
pitfalls.detail: Longer names are truncated with only a NOTICE, and two names that share their first 63 bytes collide. The limit is in bytes: ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü take two bytes each in UTF-8.

quiz.q: test_cases.last_result is kept up to date by the endpoint that records runs. A CSV import inserts into test_runs directly. What happens?
quiz.why: Nothing connects the copy to its source except the write path, and the import didn't use it. Only a reconciliation query, a trigger or a materialized view would notice.

quiz.q: order_lines.unit_price is copied from products.price when the order is placed. Is that a normalization violation?
options: Yes: the price depends on the SKU
No: it is the price agreed for that order, a different fact from today's list price
quiz.why: unit_price depends on the order line, not just the SKU. Replacing it with a join would reprice old orders.

quiz.q: A column is `updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`. A row is updated. What does updated_at hold?
options: Its old value: defaults apply only to INSERT
quiz.why: A DEFAULT is used when an INSERT omits the column (or says DEFAULT). Updates need an explicit SET or a trigger.

quiz.q: In a UTF-8 database you run `CREATE TABLE Ürünler (id int)` and then `SELECT * FROM ürünler`. What happens?
options: It works: unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive
quiz.why: Folding lower-cased only the ASCII letters, so the table is named Ürünler with a capital Ü, and ürünler is a different name.

body:
## Concept

Denormalizing means storing a fact in more than one place on purpose, usually to make
reads cheaper. Three different things go by that name, and they deserve different
treatment:

- **A derived copy**: a value you could compute from other rows (the last result of a
  test case, a count of open defects). It is a cache. It needs a source of truth, a
  mechanism that keeps it right, and a way to detect when it isn't.
- **A derived value within one row** (a line total from quantity and price). A
  generated column covers this, and the database keeps it right for you.
- **A snapshot**: a value copied at the time of an event (the price on an order line).
  It looks like a copy but records a different fact, and normalizing it away would be
  the bug.

The rest of the lesson is the boring part that makes schemas readable: naming
conventions, key naming, and the audit columns every table should carry.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Caching:** a derived column is a cache inside the database. Everything you know
  from caches applies: invalidation is the hard part, and a stale entry fails silently.
  The difference is that it can be updated in the same transaction as its source, which
  an external cache never can.
- **Java/JPA:** Hibernate's `@Formula` and a `@Transient` getter are the "compute on
  read" choice; a counter field updated in a service method is the "store it" choice,
  and every bulk JPQL `UPDATE` or native query bypasses it.
- **Go and TS:** with pgx or a query builder, the write path is a function you call. Put
  the copy's update in the same SQL statement (a data-modifying CTE), not in a second
  call that a later refactor can drop.
- **Naming:** Go wants `ProjectID`, TS wants `projectId`, SQL wants `project_id`. Keep
  each language's convention and map at the boundary (struct tags, a mapping layer);
  don't quote `"projectId"` into the database.

## Design notes

Before adding a derived copy, measure, then answer four questions in the migration's
comment: what is the source of truth; what keeps the copy right; what detects drift;
what repairs it. The mechanisms, from most to least help from the database:

1. **Generated column**, when the value comes from the same row.
2. **Composite foreign key with `ON UPDATE CASCADE`**, when the copy is a key from a
   parent row (the BCNF example in the previous lesson).
3. **Materialized view**, when a periodically refreshed result is acceptable.
4. **Trigger**, when the copy must change in the same transaction as its source and
   every writer must be covered.
5. **Application write path**, the cheapest to build and the easiest to bypass.

Conventions this codebase follows, as a starting point:

- Lower-case ASCII `snake_case` for every identifier; never quoted names.
- Plural table names (`test_runs`), which also avoids the reserved `user` and `order`.
- `id` as the primary key; `<singular>_id` for foreign keys (`project_id`).
- `_at` for `timestamptz` columns, `_on` for `date` columns, `is_`/`has_` for booleans.
- Explicit `CONSTRAINT` names wherever error mapping depends on them; otherwise the
  generated `_pkey`, `_key`, `_fkey`, `_check` names.
- `created_at`, `updated_at` and, where it matters, `created_by`/`updated_by` holding
  the application's user id. A full change history is a different tool: history tables
  (next lesson) or an audit trigger (triggers lesson).

files.examples/01_derived_copy.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.modeling.denormalize): a copy is fine once you know what keeps it honest.
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id          int  PRIMARY KEY,
  code        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  -- Denormalized: derivable from test_runs, stored so the list needs no join.
  last_result text,
  last_run_on date
);
CREATE TABLE test_runs (
  id           int  PRIMARY KEY,
  test_case_id int  NOT NULL REFERENCES test_cases,
  run_on       date NOT NULL,
  result       text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO test_cases (id, code) VALUES (1, 'TC-1'), (2, 'TC-2');

-- The one write path: record the run and move the copy forward, atomically.
WITH run AS (
  INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES (100, 1, '2026-11-02', 'failed')
  RETURNING test_case_id, run_on, result
)
UPDATE test_cases c
SET last_result = run.result, last_run_on = run.run_on
FROM run
WHERE c.id = run.test_case_id
  AND (c.last_run_on IS NULL OR c.last_run_on <= run.run_on);

-- A bulk import that doesn't know about the copy.
INSERT INTO test_runs VALUES (101, 1, '2026-11-09', 'passed'), (102, 2, '2026-11-09', 'passed');

-- Reconcile: recompute from the source and list where the copy disagrees.
CREATE VIEW latest_runs AS
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (test_case_id) test_case_id, run_on, result
  FROM test_runs
  ORDER BY test_case_id, run_on DESC, id DESC;

SELECT c.code, c.last_result AS stored, l.result AS actual
FROM test_cases c
LEFT JOIN latest_runs l ON l.test_case_id = c.id
WHERE c.last_result IS DISTINCT FROM l.result
ORDER BY c.code;

-- Repair from the same definition.
UPDATE test_cases c
SET last_result = l.result, last_run_on = l.run_on
FROM latest_runs l
WHERE l.test_case_id = c.id;
SELECT code, last_result, last_run_on FROM test_cases ORDER BY code;
files.examples/02_snapshot.sql:
-- Copying a value at the moment of an event records a different fact:
-- what was agreed then. That is not redundancy.
CREATE TABLE products (
  sku     text PRIMARY KEY,
  name    text NOT NULL,
  price   numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  vat_pct int NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  order_id   int,
  sku        text REFERENCES products,
  qty        int NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL,       -- the price on the order
  vat_pct    int NOT NULL,                  -- the KDV rate that applied
  -- Derived within the row: the database computes it, so it can't drift.
  net_total  numeric(12, 2) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price) STORED,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);
INSERT INTO products VALUES ('usb-c', 'USB-C kablo', 129.00, 18);

-- Order 1: copy price and rate from the product as part of the write.
INSERT INTO order_lines (order_id, sku, qty, unit_price, vat_pct)
SELECT 1, sku, 2, price, vat_pct FROM products WHERE sku = 'usb-c';

-- Later: a new price list, and the general KDV rate goes from 18 to 20.
UPDATE products SET price = 149.00, vat_pct = 20 WHERE sku = 'usb-c';

-- The order as invoiced, next to what a join to today's product says.
SELECT l.order_id, l.qty, l.unit_price, l.vat_pct, l.net_total,
       p.price AS price_today, p.vat_pct AS vat_today,
       l.qty * p.price AS net_if_joined
FROM order_lines l
JOIN products p USING (sku)
ORDER BY l.order_id;
